data.title: Nvidia stock falls for sixth day as Anthropic debut fails to lift shares
data.description:
Nvidia shares NVDA fell 1.5% on Thursday, reversing premarket gains of 1.9% and extending their losing streak to six consecutive trading sessions.

The chipmaker failed to benefit from the stock market debut of Anthropic, despite renewed interest in artificial intelligence stocks following the AI company's blockbuster initial public offering.

Nvidia stock declined as investors continued to assess concerns surrounding AI infrastructure spending, rising debt and uncertainty following the departure of former chief executive Jensen Huang.

Anthropic shares were trading at $98.74, down from their debut price of $111.50 but still around 19% above the IPO price of $83.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.45%, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF, which includes Nvidia, declined 1.35%.

Anthropic debut fails to lift Nvidia shares

Anthropic's IPO had initially raised hopes of renewed momentum across the AI sector.

The company priced its shares at $83, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising approximately $81.3 billion.

The listing could indirectly benefit Nvidia by providing Anthropic with additional capital to invest in computing infrastructure.

Higher spending on AI training and inference could translate into greater demand for Nvidia's chips.

However, that potential benefit did not provide immediate support for the stock on Thursday.

Nvidia has been under pressure as investors reassess the sustainability of the AI investment cycle.

The stock has fallen 38% since reaching a record closing high of $239.24 on October 6, as concerns about infrastructure spending and financing requirements have weighed on sentiment.

The company also faces uncertainty following Huang's resignation last week.

Reports concerning allegations involving the former CEO and a woman accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset have added to the negative sentiment surrounding the chipmaker.

Nvidia's latest earnings and revenue forecast were strong, but the results were not enough to reverse the stock's decline.

Hedge funds show mixed positioning in Nvidia

Institutional investor filings for the third quarter of 2026 showed that several prominent hedge funds increased or maintained their exposure to Nvidia, although some investors reduced their positions.

Tiger Global raised its Nvidia holdings to 12 million shares from 11.2 million, while Altimeter increased its position to 10.01 million shares from 9.41 million.

Senator Investment Group also expanded its stake to 444,000 shares from 337,000.

Third Point initiated a new position, acquiring 1.5 million shares, while Corvex Management maintained its holding of 16,000 shares.

However, Soros Capital reduced its Nvidia position to 10,000 shares from 77,000.

Soros Fund also cut its holdings to 859,000 shares from 1.06 million.

The mixed positioning suggests that institutional investors had differing views on the chipmaker's prospects during the quarter.

Analyst upgrades Nvidia to Buy

Despite the recent decline, Seeking Alpha analyst Lee Bailey upgraded Nvidia to Buy from a previously more cautious stance following the company's third-quarter results.

Bailey cited the earnings beat, improved cash conversion and a higher fiscal 2028 growth outlook.

The analyst believes the market is undervaluing Nvidia's growth prospects.

Bailey set a 12-month price target of $235, implying approximately 50% upside.

The upgrade suggests analysts still see value in Nvidia despite recent weakness.

However, the stock's performance suggests that strong financial results and positive analyst views have yet to outweigh concerns about the AI investment cycle and uncertainty surrounding the company's leadership.

data.title: Aswath Damodaran values Anthropic at $76 a share, below its $83 IPO price
data.description:
Aswath Damodaran, the New York University finance professor widely known as the 'Dean of Valuation', estimates Anthropic's intrinsic value at approximately $76 per share, below the artificial intelligence company's $83 initial public offering (IPO) price.

In an updated valuation published ahead of the company's Nasdaq debut, Damodaran estimated Anthropic's aggregate equity value at approximately $1.35 trillion.

His calculations incorporated the company's latest financial results, higher computing costs and the possibility of tighter AI regulations.

Anthropic raised $81 billion in its IPO, making it the largest offering of all time.

The company priced its shares at $83 apiece, above its initial guidance range of $70 to $78.

The stock opened on Nasdaq at $111.50 under the ticker ANT giving it a $2 trillion valuation, before giving up some gains to trade at $96.33 at the time of writing.

Damodaran's assessment suggests that the stock's offering price was already above his estimated intrinsic value, while its subsequent market price represented a further premium.

Damodaran lowers Anthropic valuation over rising costs and regulatory risks

Damodaran had initially valued Anthropic's equity at approximately $1.475 trillion in a November 2 analysis.

However, developments over the following 15 days prompted him to revise his assumptions.

The updated prospectus provided third-quarter financial information, while the US midterm election results raised questions about the future economics of the AI industry.

In particular, Damodaran expects data centres to become more expensive to build and AI regulations to become more stringent.

He reduced his assumption for sales generated per dollar of capital invested during the first five years from $3 to $2.75, reflecting higher expected infrastructure spending.

He also increased the anticipated regulatory drag on operating margins, adjusting his assumptions from 5% to 6%, with the target operating margin set at 26.5%.

Damodaran explained that these changes would increase the company's reinvestment requirements and reduce its expected cash flows.

"I do not want to overreact to the election results, but I do think it is prudent to assume that building data centers will become more expensive," he wrote.

Share count complicates Anthropic's intrinsic value calculation

A significant part of Damodaran's analysis focused on the difficulty of determining Anthropic's actual share count.

He argued that the presence of multiple share classes, restricted stock, and employee stock options makes it difficult to arrive at an accurate per-share valuation.

According to his analysis, Anthropic's share count could range from approximately 14.88 billion shares under the primary share method to 17.68 billion under the fully diluted approach.

The company has 1.026 billion restricted shares subject to a four-year vesting period and 1.774 billion outstanding options, of which 1.082 billion are already vested.

Damodaran argued that simply using either the primary or fully diluted share count could produce misleading results.

Instead, he favours an option-adjusted approach, which estimates the value of outstanding options and deducts that amount from aggregate equity value before dividing it by the primary and restricted shares.

"I would suggest viewing the option-adjusted value per share as the number closest to the truth," he wrote.

His calculations produced a range of values, with the primary share approach generating a higher estimate and the fully diluted method producing a lower one.

The option-adjusted valuation stood at approximately $76 per share, compared with the $83 IPO price.

Anthropic's growth prospects underpin long-term valuation

Despite the downward revision, Damodaran's valuation model assumes substantial growth for Anthropic over the coming years.

His assumptions project revenue growth of 190% in the next year, followed by 42% annual growth during years two to five.

Revenue growth subsequently moderates as the company matures.

The model also assumes that operating margins will improve as the company gains pricing power from premium AI products and computing costs grow more slowly than revenues.

Damodaran expects Anthropic's operating margin to reach 26.5% over time, while its cost of capital gradually declines as the company becomes more established.

His analysis also considers the substantial computing commitments the company has made, including lease, purchase, and infrastructure obligations.

He incorporated a 10% probability of failure into the valuation to account for the risks associated with those commitments.

Beyond the financial assumptions, Damodaran raised concerns about Anthropic's unusual voting structure.

He noted that a founder-owned share carries 50.01% of voting rights in perpetuity.

He compared the arrangement with government-held golden shares in privatised companies, arguing that concentrating such significant voting power in a single share could create risks.

Overall, Damodaran's analysis highlights the distinction between Anthropic's long-term growth potential and the price investors are willing to pay for its shares.

While his model anticipates substantial revenue expansion and improving profitability, higher infrastructure costs, regulatory uncertainty, and share dilution remain important considerations in assessing its valuation.

data.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei defends $900B AI spending and safety strategy after IPO
data.description:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei outlined the company's long-term growth strategy, artificial intelligence (AI) safety priorities and path to profitability following its stock market debut on Thursday.

Speaking to CNBC after the company's initial public offering (IPO), the siblings discussed how Anthropic intends to balance its rapid expansion with responsible AI development, rising computing costs and the expectations of public-market investors.

Anthropic sees long-term value in balancing growth with AI safety

Dario Amodei said the company's understanding of scaling laws helped establish the potential of AI models, although the economic implications became clearer only as the technology developed.

He described the company's approach to pacing AI development as a way to balance technological progress with safety considerations.

"We could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely," Amodei said, explaining the company's approach to developing increasingly capable models.

He argued that this strategy could also benefit investors over the longer term, as companies that establish trust with customers and enterprises could be better positioned to succeed.

"The company that builds the safest, that has trust of the customers and the enterprises of the world, I think that is the company that's going to be both best for society and, in the long run, I hope, best for the performance of the company," he added.

Daniela Amodei also highlighted the company's public benefit corporation structure, which legally requires it to balance shareholder interests with its commitment to public benefit.

She said the structure reflects the founders' intention to build a company that generates economic value while ensuring its technology benefits society.

She added that Anthropic considers safety a central part of its mission and believes the technology carries both significant opportunities and real risks.

"Anthropic has been a safety company, a safety-first company from day one," Daniela Amodei said. "The promise is incredible, and the risks are real."

Frontier AI models and computing costs remain central to strategy

Discussing competition from OpenAI, open-weight models and technology companies developing their own AI systems, Dario Amodei said Anthropic believes the biggest economic opportunities remain concentrated at the AI frontier.

He argued that improvements in cognitive capabilities can unlock applications beyond chatbots, including coding, biology and robotics.

"The economic value of things further along the frontier is so much larger than things earlier in the frontier that that's where most of the value accumulates," he said.

He also said developing frontier models gives Anthropic an advantage in producing smaller and more efficient models that can compete on price.

As an example, he cited the company's Haiku 5.5 model, saying Anthropic had reduced its price by four times compared with Haiku 4.5.

Meanwhile, Daniela Amodei addressed concerns about the infrastructure required to support the company's expansion.

She said Anthropic wants local communities to have a voice in data centre development and stressed that additional electricity costs should not be passed on to consumers.

"We have already committed to matching whatever price differential might happen from an electricity grid perspective, we pay for," she said.

Dario Amodei addresses $900B commitments and profitability

Anthropic has $900 billion in infrastructure commitments, which is expected to put pressure on its path to profitability.

Dario Amodei said the spending commitments were spread across several years and don't look large when compared to the cash the company has and the revenue it's making.

"If you look at the amount of cash we have on the balance sheet and the amount of revenue that we're already making per year, suddenly, those commitments don't seem so large," he said.

Amodei said Anthropic generally tries to estimate its computing requirements conservatively and purchase additional capacity from the spot market when necessary.

However, he maintained that spending on research and development and training more capable models remained worthwhile because of the economic returns the company had historically generated.

"The returns to that are so high that we are willing to put in place these very large compute spends because, historically, we have seen over and over again that it pays off," he added.

The CEO also discussed the possibility of using debt financing in the future.

He said Anthropic hoped to achieve an investment-grade credit rating and viewed debt as a financing instrument it could eventually use.

On the subject of partnerships, Daniela Amodei highlighted the company's relationships with Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, saying access to multiple computing partners had been a strategic advantage.

Dario Amodei also said the company was satisfied with its work with SpaceX, which provides computing capacity.

Addressing investor expectations following the IPO, the CEO said Anthropic would remain focused on its underlying business rather than short-term share price movements.

"We always want to under promise and overdeliver," he said, describing a principle that guides the company's internal operations and its approach to investors.

He added that the long-term fundamentals of the business mattered more than daily, weekly or monthly market movements.

Anthropic raised $81 billion in its IPO, making it the largest offering of all time.

The company priced its shares at $83 apiece, above its initial guidance range of $70 to $78.

The stock opened on Nasdaq at $111.50, under the ticker ANT.

The stock gave up some gains and was trading at $98.32 at the time of writing.

The strong debut marked an important milestone for the AI company, which has attracted significant investor interest amid growing concerns about the sustainability of technology companies' AI spending.

Investors looking to buy the shares of the AI Lab can read our guide on how to buy Anthropic stock.

data.title: Best Trading Platforms to Buy Anthropic Stock (ANT)
data.description:
Anthropic's shares are now on the Nasdaq. We compare the best places to buy ANT.

The best trading platforms to buy Anthropic stock are now live with ANT. The maker of Claude priced its IPO at $83 on 18 November, above its $70–$78 range, and opened on the Nasdaq at $111.50, up 34.3%.

Here are the platforms we'd use, and what to check before your first order.

Quick answer: where can I buy Anthropic stock?

You can buy ANT on any platform that offers Nasdaq-listed US shares and has added the stock. All five of our picks let you own the real shares, with fractional investing:

  1. eToro, best for beginners: the simplest app we've tested, with zero-commission US shares.
  2. Webull, best for trading around the open and close: zero commission, strong charts and pre- and after-market trading.
  3. Moomoo, best for research: zero-commission US shares with Level 2 data and analyst tools.
  4. Public, best for a simple, social app: a clean interface and a feed where investors share their views.
  5. Interactive Brokers, best for large orders: the lowest costs here, plus cheap currency conversion.

Real shares or CFD? Every platform above lets you own ANT outright, which is what most people want from a long-term holding. Some brokers also offer ANT as a CFD, where you only take a position on the price, usually with leverage, and pay a fee for every night you keep it open. That only makes sense for short-term trading, and on a brand-new listing the swings can be big in both directions.

Best trading platforms to buy Anthropic stock

1. eToro

eToro is the easiest way we've found to buy a US stock: search ANT, type an amount and confirm. US shares are commission-free and fractional, so you don't need $111.50 to get started. Its CopyTrader feed also shows how other investors are positioning in ANT, which is useful context on a debut this hyped.

2. Webull

Webull charges no commission on US shares and lets you trade before the open and after the close. On a debut where the price can gap overnight, that matters. Its charting is among the best in a free app.

3. Moomoo

Moomoo combines zero-commission trading with research tools you'd normally pay for, including Level 2 data and analyst estimates. It's a good fit if you want to follow ANT's order flow closely in its first weeks.

4. Public

Public keeps things simple: a clean app, fractional shares and a feed where investors share their views on stocks like ANT. It suits first-time investors who want to start small.

5. Interactive Brokers

Interactive Brokers has the lowest costs here for bigger orders, plus very cheap currency conversion if you're funding in a currency other than dollars. Its platform is more complex, but it's hard to beat on price.

How to buy Anthropic shares in four steps

Here's the short version. Our full guide on how to buy Anthropic stock goes through each step in more detail.

  1. Open an account with one of the platforms above. You'll need ID and proof of address. If you live outside the US, you'll also sign a W-8BEN form, which cuts US withholding tax on any future dividends.
  2. Fund it. A bank transfer is usually free. If you fund in a currency other than dollars, check the conversion fee: it can cost more than the trade itself.
  3. Search for ANT. Check it reads Anthropic, Nasdaq. Ignore anything labelled "pre-IPO", "tokenised" or "Anthropic exposure" if you want the actual listed shares.
  4. Use a limit order. New listings can move several percent in minutes. A limit order sets the most you'll pay, while a market order fills at whatever price is available, which in a fast market can be well above the last quote.

What you're actually paying for

Two numbers explain most of the debate around ANT. Revenue has grown roughly thirteenfold in a year, which is almost unheard of at this size. But Anthropic has also signed up for close to $900 billion of future computing spend, so it needs that growth to keep going for years.

IPO price vs your price

IPO investors paid $83. Everyone else buys at the market price, which opened at $111.50. That 34.3% jump on the first trade means anyone buying now is already paying well above what IPO investors paid.

There's no prize for buying on day one. Big listings often swing hard in their first weeks as IPO investors take profits and new buyers arrive. If you like the business, buying in two or three smaller slices over a few weeks takes the pressure off getting the timing right.

For the full story of the listing, from the first filing to the final price, see our Anthropic IPO page.

Dates to watch

  • Index reviews: MSCI could add ANT to its indices at an upcoming review if it meets the eligibility rules, which would bring buying from funds that track them.
  • Nasdaq-100: a fast-track entry is possible, according to Bloomberg.
  • First earnings as a public company: the date hasn't been announced yet.
  • Lock-up expiry: insiders are typically barred from selling for around 180 days after an IPO. When that ends, a wave of extra shares can hit the market.

What to know about your vote

Public shareholders get Class A shares, but control stays with the founders. Anthropic's Founder LLC is expected to hold 50.1% of the votes, and the strategic investors' Class N shares carry no votes at all. Anthropic is also a Public Benefit Corporation, which means its board weighs its safety mission alongside shareholder returns. If you want a say in how a company is run, ANT doesn't offer much of one.

Bull case vs bear case

Bull case: few companies have ever listed growing this fast. Claude has become a default tool for businesses and developers, and Anthropic is one of only a handful of companies able to build frontier AI models. Index inclusion could add steady buying in the first weeks.

Bear case: at around $1.5 trillion, the market is pricing in years of near-flawless execution. Compute commitments are enormous, OpenAI, Google, Meta and xAI are all spending heavily, and early-November's sell-off in AI and chip stocks showed how quickly sentiment can turn.

Other ways to get Anthropic exposure

  • Alphabet (GOOGL) owned around 14% of Anthropic before the IPO, and Amazon (AMZN) has invested billions since 2023. Both give you indirect exposure, though Anthropic is a small part of much bigger businesses.
  • AI and tech ETFs are likely to add ANT over time, and spread your money across many AI names instead of one new listing.

FAQs

Is Anthropic on the stock market?

Yes. Anthropic went public on 19 November 2026, and its Class A shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

What is ANT stock?

ANT is the ticker for Anthropic, PBC, the company behind the Claude AI models. It's listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. Don't confuse it with other companies or tokens using "ANT" in their name.

What is Anthropic's stock price?

ANT opened at $111.50 on its first day, 34.3% above its IPO price of $83. The price moves throughout the trading day, so check a live quote on your broker before you buy.

When can I buy Anthropic stock?

Now. ANT has traded on the Nasdaq since 19 November 2026, so you can buy it during US market hours, and before the open or after the close on platforms that offer extended-hours trading, such as Webull.

Where can I buy Anthropic stock?

On any broker that offers Nasdaq-listed US shares and has added ANT. Our top picks are eToro, Webull, Moomoo, Public and Interactive Brokers. Anthropic's US IPO brokers, Fidelity, Schwab, Robinhood, SoFi and E*TRADE, also offer it.

Can I buy Anthropic stock on Robinhood?

Yes. Robinhood was one of the brokers handling Anthropic's IPO for retail investors, and it offers ANT now that the shares are trading.

What was Anthropic's IPO price?

$83 a share, set on 18 November 2026. That was above the $70–$78 range Anthropic marketed to investors.

Can you buy Anthropic stock before the IPO?

Not any more, and you don't need to. Now that ANT is listed, you can buy the real shares at the market price. Be wary of any product still sold as "pre-IPO" Anthropic exposure.

How much does it cost to invest in Anthropic?

Less than one share, if you want. Most of the platforms above offer fractional shares, so you can start with as little as $10, and eToro, Webull, Moomoo and Public charge no commission on US stocks. If you fund in another currency, check the conversion fee.

Does Google own 14% of Anthropic?

Alphabet, Google's parent company, owned around 14% of Anthropic before the IPO, with its stake capped at 15%. It was also among the tech companies that bought into the $26 billion placement at the IPO price.

Is Anthropic overpriced?

That's the main debate. At around $1.5 trillion at its opening price, ANT trades at a large multiple of its sales, which already assumes years of very fast growth. Supporters point to revenue rising roughly thirteenfold in a year. Sceptics point to nearly $900 billion of compute commitments and heavy competition.

Should I buy Anthropic stock?

It depends on your goals and how much risk you can take. Anthropic is one of the fastest-growing companies ever to list, but new listings are volatile and the valuation leaves little room for disappointment. Many investors build a position gradually rather than buying all at once on day one.

Final thoughts

Anthropic is one of the most important companies of the AI era, and for the first time anyone can own a piece of it. eToro is our top pick for buying ANT, Webull is a strong alternative for active investors, and IBKR wins on cost for larger orders. Whichever you choose, a great company is not automatically a great investment at any price. A small position, built gradually, is a sensible way to start.

data.title: Bloom Energy stock rises as BMO upgrade and Anthropic IPO lift shares
data.description:
Bloom Energy shares BE gained 6% on Thursday after BMO Capital upgraded the stock, citing stronger confidence in the company's commercial traction and execution.

Renewed investor interest in artificial intelligence infrastructure following Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering also supported sentiment toward power-related stocks.

BMO raised its rating on Bloom Energy to Outperform from Market Perform, although it lowered its price target to $230 from $260.

The reduction reflects recent multiple compression across power infrastructure companies rather than a deterioration in the firm's assessment of Bloom Energy's business prospects.

The upgrade followed a non-deal roadshow involving Bloom Energy CFO Simon Edwards and Vice President of Investor Relations Michael Tierney.

Following the meetings, BMO analysts said they had greater conviction in the company's commercial progress and recent execution.

The analysts also said their estimates pointed to potential upside relative to consensus expectations for 2027.

Although the stock gained 6% initially, it lost most of the gains and was trading up 3% at the time of writing.

BMO sees upside despite lower price target

BMO's revised rating indicates a more positive view of Bloom Energy shares despite the lower valuation target.

The brokerage said the stock was "ready for takeoff" as it upgraded the shares to Outperform.

It also noted that its decision followed discussions with company executives during the investor roadshow.

The new $230 target represents a reduction from the previous $260 level.

BMO attributed the adjustment to lower valuation multiples across the power infrastructure sector, reflecting broader market conditions.

However, the analysts' assessment of Bloom Energy's commercial traction and execution remained positive.

Their analysis suggests that the company's earnings potential could exceed current market expectations for 2027.

Bloom Energy develops solid-oxide fuel cell systems designed to provide reliable, on-site electricity.

These systems have attracted attention as data centre operators and technology companies seek dependable power sources to support growing AI infrastructure requirements.

Anthropic IPO renews interest in AI power infrastructure

The upgrade came as investors returned to AI-related stocks following Anthropic's IPO.

The AI company raised approximately $81.3 billion by selling around 980 million shares at a price that valued it at roughly $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic is set to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

The offering was larger than SpaceX's initial $75 billion fundraising.

Following the exercise of an overallotment option, SpaceX's IPO proceeds reached $85.7 billion.

Anthropic's underwriters also hold an option to purchase up to 147 million additional shares.

If fully exercised, the option could increase the IPO proceeds to approximately $93.5 billion.

The scale of the listing has renewed investor interest in companies supporting the AI infrastructure buildout.

Power suppliers are among the potential beneficiaries, as data centres require reliable electricity to operate increasingly demanding computing systems.

Bloom Energy's on-site fuel cell technology places it within this broader investment theme.

The renewed interest in AI infrastructure stocks provided an additional tailwind for its shares on Thursday.

Manufacturing recognition

Bloom Energy also announced a separate development on Wednesday, saying it had been named among America's Top Manufacturers of 2027 by TIME and Statista.

The ranking recognises 250 leading US manufacturers based on financial performance, innovation capacity and employment metrics.

Overall, the combination of BMO's more positive assessment, renewed enthusiasm for AI infrastructure, and the company's manufacturing recognition supported Bloom Energy shares.

Investors will continue to assess whether its commercial momentum can translate into results that exceed current market expectations.

data.title: Anthropic's ANT closes at $97.17, up 17% on its first day of trading
data.description:
Anthropic’s Class A shares, ticker ANT, closed at $97.17 on their first day on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on 19 November 2026.

That is about 17% above the $83.00 IPO price set a day earlier, and about 13% below the $111.50 opening print.

The day began in Times Square, where co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell at 9:30am ET. The ceremony itself did not start trading in ANT. The first trade came later, at 16:50 GMT (11:50am ET), when the shares opened at $111.50, about 34% above the offering price.

Indications had been climbing through the morning, from about $99.60 to $105, then $110 and $111, before the stock opened slightly above that last level. The early burst did not last.

ANT peaked at $115.10 just before noon ET and slipped as low as $92.72.

By mid-afternoon the shares were changing hands around $95.60, still about 15% above the IPO price. The $97.17 close left the debut comfortably above the offering, but well short of the opening pop.

Even so, a 17% first-day gain on the largest IPO on record is a strong debut, the more so on a session in which the main US indexes finished more than 2% lower. The market took some of the opening froth off, but buyers who received stock at $83 still ended the day well in the money.

More than 846 million shares changed hands, ahead of the 522 million traded on SpaceX’s opening day in June, and enough to make ANT the most actively traded name on the Nasdaq. Volume had already passed 640 million by mid-session.

At the $111.50 open, Reuters put Anthropic’s market value at about $2 trillion, a level exceeded by only a handful of US-listed firms, and ahead of the $1.96 trillion it assigned to SpaceX at its June opening trade. That is a reported valuation at the open, not a closing figure.

The fade came as the wider market turned lower. US stocks ended more than 2% down. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,101.11 points, or 2.19%, to 49,097.06, the S&P 500 fell 2.02% to 7,175.83, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to 23,879.20.

AI shares were mixed as investors weighed worries about higher interest rates. The Nasdaq itself had been up as much as 2% after the open before those gains were given back.

The listing is the first by a frontier AI lab and sets a public-market benchmark for the group, with OpenAI still private. Ordinary investors now have a listed way to take a direct view on a stand-alone model developer, rather than only through the chipmakers and cloud groups that have dominated the trade.

Anthropic sold 980 million Class A shares at $83.00 on Wednesday, of which 956,351,354 were sold by the company and 23,648,646 by selling stockholders. The deal raised about $81.3 billion, making it the largest initial public offering on record, above SpaceX’s initial $75 billion.

The size and price had already been lifted once before the open. Last week the company had marketed 825 million shares at $70 to $78; on Wednesday it sold more stock, and at a higher price, than that range implied. SpaceX later reached $85.7 billion after its overallotment was exercised.

Anthropic’s underwriters have the option to buy up to a further 147 million Class A shares, which would bring in another $12.2 billion and take the IPO total to $93.5 billion if exercised. They have until 20 November to take up that option. The offering itself is expected to close on 20 November, subject to customary conditions.

The banks on the deal are due about $550 million in underwriting fees, according to the company’s filing, more than the roughly $500 million paid on the SpaceX IPO.

The company priced the offering above its marketed range and increased the number of shares being sold, initially valuing the Claude developer at $1.5 trillion. Investors who received an allocation pay the $83 offering price. Anyone buying once the shares are listed pays the market price, which closed at $97.17.

Demand was unusually lopsided. Retail interest in the IPO was the largest in history. Anthropic prioritized institutional investors it already knew, and roughly half of the firms that placed orders were left empty-handed, a higher share than usual.

Retail allocation came in at around 15%, below the roughly 20% the company had targeted, though still above the 5% to 10% typical in most IPOs.

Analysts who opened coverage stayed above the close. Melius started at Buy with a $155 price target; Ben Reitzes, the firm’s head of technology research, said that assigned value could even be “conservative”. Needham’s Scott Berg has a Buy rating and a $150 target. The average target across five Buy ratings was about $116.

Wolfe Research, in a Thursday note, said cybersecurity could match Anthropic’s coding opportunity and reach $500 billion annually.

The company has given a sense of the scale behind that interest. In its prospectus, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion of revenue in the nine months to 30 September, up about 1,200% from the same period a year earlier, and that its run-rate revenue was about $81 billion by the end of October.

What comes next is tightly timetabled. Index funds will not add the stock immediately. The Morningstar US Total Market Index will include it after five trading days, the Nasdaq-100 after 18 December, and the S&P 500 will not add it for at least a year.

About 15.5 billion insider shares are subject to lock-up agreements that run until after Anthropic reports results in the third quarter of next year. No date has been set for the first earnings report.

The official terms of the offering are in our report on Anthropic’s official IPO pricing. The first print is covered in our report on how ANT opened.

data.title: Pershing Square stock drops as valuation concerns weigh on Bill Ackman’s fund
data.description:
Pershing Square stock continued its strong sell-off on Thursday, reaching its lowest level since August. PS has dropped by over 42% from the year-to-date high. This article explores whether Bill Ackman’s company is a good investment as the stock drops.

Pershing Square’s business is under pressure this year

Bill Ackman’s hedge fund is facing substantial pressure this year as most of its portfolio companies continue falling. Uber Technologies stock dropped to $65 today, down by 25% from its highest point this year. It has fallen by 35% from its all-time high. 

Netflix stockhas also plunged this year as the company’s revenue growth stalls. The company lacks a clear catalyst as its user and engagement growth fades. Brookfield has also fallen by 18% from the year-to-date high.

Other top companies in its portfolio, like Microsoft, Meta Platforms, and S&P Global have also pulled back in the past few days. In total, the company’s return this year has underperformed the market. Its portfolio has dropped by 6% this year, underperforming the broader market and the SCHD ETF. 

The most recent results showed that its business slowed in the third quarter as its management fees dropped. Total revenue dropped to over $56 million from $66.1 million in the same period last year. Its management fee fell to $56 million from $62.3 million. It did not make any performance fees. 

The company made a net loss of $19 million after making a $155 million in profit in the same period last year. 

For starters, Pershing Square Inc. makes money from the management fees it receives from its fee paying assets under management (FPAUM), the preferred performance fees it receives from Pershing Square Holdings and Pershing Square International, and the service fees paid by Howard Hughes Holdings, a company it controls. 

A key concern about Pershing Square’s stock is that the company is highly overvalued since it has a market capitalization of over $16 billion against its fee-paying assets under management of $23 billion, up by 4% from the same period last year. 98% of these funds is permanent capital.

In contrast, Blue Owl Capital, a top player in the private equity and private credit industries, has a market cap of $14.2 billion against $330 billion in assets under management. Similarly, Carlyle Group has $479 billion in assets and a market cap of $13 billion. 

Pershing Square stock price analysis

PS stock chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that the PS stock has come under pressure in the past few weeks. It has slumped from the October high of $60 to a low of $35 today. 

The stock has dropped below the important support level of $42.20, its lowest level on October 22nd. It has also moved to the 61.8% Fibonacci Retracement level. 

Pershing Square has moved below the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) and the Supertrend indicator. Therefore, the stock will likely drop further, potentially to the psychological level of $30. On the other hand, a move above $42 will invalidate the bearish outlook.

data.title: Temu owner just cut its marketing bill: stock is soaring
data.description:
PDD Holdings (PDD) shares are soaring on Nov. 19 after the Temu owner beat third-quarter profit expectations.

The surprise came from the expense side of the ledger.

PDD spent a whopping 5 billion yuan less on sales and marketing than it did a year earlier, even as revenue held steady.

That was sufficient to spark a rally in PDD stock that had lost more than 30% for the year as of its previous close.  

The next question is whether PDD can get sales growing again while keeping more of each yuan it brings in.

PDD stock rips higher on better-than-expected quarter

PDD’s adjusted earnings of 21.04 yuan per American depositary share beat the 18.54 yuan analysts expected by about 13%.

They were nearly unchanged from 21.08 yuan a year earlier.

Wall Street consensus had priced in a more pronounced earnings decline, which helps explain why a broadly flat result could move the PDD shares so sharply.

The savings were sizable.

Excluding share-based compensation, sales and marketing fell to 23% of revenue from 28% a year earlier.

Meanwhile, research and development spending rose to 5.1 billion yuan from 4.3 billion yuan.

PDD still has room to decide where it spends, and the quarter showed how much that choice can matter to margins even when sales stall.

Temu’s cheap-parcel model faces a new test

Flat revenue masked two businesses moving in opposite directions.

Online marketing services and other revenue grew 12%, while transaction services fell 12%.

The latter is a groupwide figure that includes fees tied to Temu, making it worth watching as trade rules change the economics of selling cheap goods across borders.

In July, the European Union introduced a €3 customs duty per product category in qualifying shipments worth less than €150.

A fixed charge takes a larger bite out of a cheap item’s price, leaving less room to pass it on without weakening the bargain.

On Thursday’s call, co-CEO Lei Chen said PDD is expanding shared warehousing and logistics so merchants can stock goods closer to shoppers.

Can PDD shares sustain the post-earnings rally?

PDD ended September with 455.4 billion yuan in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, giving it room to fund that logistics push.

Operating cash flow, however, slipped to 43 billion yuan from 45.7 billion yuan a year earlier.

That makes cash generation worth following alongside adjusted earnings as PDD builds out its fulfillment network.

The next earnings report gives investors two concrete markers.

A smaller decline in transaction services would suggest that side of the business is stabilizing.

If the marketing bill also stays near 23% of sales, PDD would be making progress on both fronts.

That combination would give Thursday’s rally something more durable to build on.

data.title: Anthropic pops 34% to cross $2 trillion valuation in historic Nasdaq debut
data.description:
Anthropic ANT made its stock market debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday at $111.50 per share, raising more than $81 billion in what is the largest initial public offering on record.

Shares jumped 34.3% after opening, pushing the artificial intelligence company's market valuation above $2 trillion.

This placed Anthropic behind only Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet and Amazon in terms of market capitalization.

The IPO carries significant implications for the AI trade, as Anthropic becomes the first major AI lab to go public. Analysts expect Anthropic shares to become a proxy for the broader AI trade.

The listing comes at a time when concerns are mounting over the sustainability of the AI boom, with questions further intensifying amid the ongoing Nvidia leadership turmoil.

The Claude maker sold 980 million shares at an IPO price of $83 apiece, above the previously marketed range of $70 to $78.

The stock is trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

The IPO was led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, with JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Barclays also listed in the prospectus as underwriters.

Anthropic reiterates commitment to AI safety

Anthropic co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell, marking the public listing of the company behind the Claude chatbot.

Dario Amodei used the occasion to reiterate the company's commitment to AI safety, saying: "We will not bend to either business or political pressure."

He also pledged that Anthropic would remain "obsessed with safety" as it seeks to avoid potentially catastrophic risks associated with artificial intelligence.

The debut comes as investors continue to assess how much value can be created by companies developing increasingly powerful AI models, even as concerns persist over the scale of spending required to train and operate them.

Nasdaq rules could provide another boost

Anthropic could receive a further boost from changes to Nasdaq's index inclusion rules introduced earlier this year.

The revised methodology allows large-cap companies to qualify for fast-track inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 after just 15 days of trading.

The change was implemented before SpaceX's June listing and could accelerate demand from passive funds tracking the benchmark.

Research group Intropic estimates that index-tracking funds will purchase around 333 million Anthropic shares across four dates during the first month of trading.

That represents approximately 30% of the 1.1 billion shares in the offering, including the greenshoe option.

Anthropic revenue surges as losses widen

Anthropic filed its prospectus last month, revealing a sharp acceleration in revenue, which surged around 1,200% during the first nine months of the year.

For the first half of 2026, the filing showed revenue of $16.29 billion, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier.

The company's reported net loss for the first half of 2026 was $80.748 billion, compared with a net loss of $41.965 billion for the full year 2025.

While the headline figures appear alarming, much of the reported loss was attributed to an accounting practice.

data.title: AMD stock falls 7% as Hunterbrook alleges links to blacklisted Chinese firm
data.description:
AMD stock fell 7% on Thursday after Hunterbrook Media, an investigative publication affiliated with short seller Hunterbrook Capital, alleged that the chipmaker's firmware was being used by a blacklisted Chinese company and three businesses linked to it.

The report claimed that IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker, had incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products after being placed on the US government's export blacklist.

Hunterbrook also alleged that three other server companies with links to IEIT offered products containing closely matching firmware, raising questions about whether servers designed by the blacklisted company were being sold through other businesses.

The revelations were made in a report called 'AMD has its own China problem'.

Hunterbrook Media disclosed that, at the time of publication, its affiliated investment firm Hunterbrook Capital was short AMD shares and held long positions in a basket of comparable securities.

The report drew parallels with the controversy surrounding Nvidia's sales of advanced chips to Chinese companies and questioned whether AMD could genuinely be considered a safer alternative to its larger rival.

AMD's China exposure comes under scrutiny

The firm has questioned a growing perception that AMD is a less risky way to gain exposure to the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom amid scrutiny of Nvidia's China business.

The firm highlighted that AMD shares gained nearly 45% in the five sessions through November 12, the day Nvidia announced CEO Jensen Huang's resignation in what CNBC reported was a board decision to oust him.

William Blair and Oppenheimer also upgraded AMD during that period, according to Hunterbrook.

However, the publication argued that investors may be underestimating AMD's exposure to the same geopolitical and regulatory risks facing Nvidia.

As of the November 18 close, AMD traded at around 30 times its estimated earnings for the next fiscal year, compared with approximately nine times for Nvidia, based on analyst estimates published by Yahoo Finance.

"The Bear Cave believes investors are trading one cousin’s problems for the other’s," the report said, referring to Jensen Huang's relationship with AMD chief Lisa Su, who is his cousin.

The Bear Cave is an investigative newsletter owned by Hunterbrook Media.

IEIT allegedly used AMD firmware after blacklisting

Hunterbrook said the US Commerce Department placed IEIT on its Entity List in March 2025.

The designation means that exports of items covered by US export controls to the company require a licence, with the department's stated policy being to deny such applications.

Despite the restrictions, IEIT has incorporated at least six newer versions of AMD's firmware into its products since being blacklisted, according to the investigation.

The latest version identified by Hunterbrook appeared in an updated product listing posted on October 19.

The report also identified three companies that sell servers built around AMD chips under their own brands: Maginfra in China, Kaytus in Singapore and Aivres in California.

"Hunterbrook found that the firmware they offer is nearly identical to IEIT’s, suggesting they may be selling servers designed by the blacklisted company. Corporate filings point the same way: IEIT’s 2022 annual report listed Aivres, then called Inspur Systems, as a subsidiary. Kaytus’s own audited accounts name IEIT as its ultimate parent company," it said.

The investigation also highlighted other alleged links between AMD and entities subject to US restrictions.

Hunterbrook said AMD reported $67 million in licensing income in 2025 that the publication traced to two Chinese chip ventures blacklisted in 2019.

It also identified a server from Cancon, an alias of the blacklisted company Suma, in AMD's February 2026 product catalogue.

"In sum: AMD appears no less at risk from China chip restrictions than Nvidia, despite the recent surge of positive coverage," Hunterbrook said.

Potential changes to export rules could add pressure

The report also warned that changes to US export regulations could expose AMD to additional restrictions on its international business.

A suspension of a rule that would extend export restrictions to foreign companies at least 50% owned by blacklisted entities is due to expire on January 10, 2027.

If implemented, the provision could expand restrictions to Kaytus and other foreign companies in which IEIT holds at least a 50% stake, it said.

Separately, a newly released interim final rule, which takes effect on Thursday, will require licences for advanced chips shipped to Singapore and four other countries.

The potential impact on AMD could be significant given its business in the region.

The company recorded $4.28 billion in billings to customers in Singapore during fiscal 2025, accounting for more than 10% of its total sales.

"For AMD, this could mean additional licensing requirements that can delay or block sales," Hunterbrook said.
